results.message: Did your people believe outsiders were going to hell?

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
Cyprian said plainly that no one is saved outside the Church. He wrote it about heretics, people who confessed Christ but stood outside our communion. Even one who died for confessing Christ is not helped if he is outside. He gave the reason: there is no salvation out of the Church. Yet he pressed the same man to turn while he lived.

Augustine taught that the punishment of the lost has no end. He would not let them say the punishment ends.

Cyprian did not write of people who never heard of Christ. We do not claim to know what he would have said of them.

glosses.plain_meaning: For us, communion is a formal standing within the one body. You can lose it, and be given it back. At the council of 256, Cyprian said no one would be put out of it for thinking differently.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, communion is a real standing inside the one body. You can lose it, and be given it back. Cyprian held that it should survive sharp disagreement.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener is likely to hear either a specific liturgical rite -- going up to receive -- or a general warmth of fellowship, and the second makes disagreement look like a failure of communion. We mean a formal, structural status of standing within the body, with public consequences, that, on Cyprian's own principle, disagreement should not dissolve. Disagreement is expected among us; what would break communion is not arguing but separating.
false_friend: a specific liturgical rite alone, going up to receive, with no broader sense of standing attached
a general warmth of fellowship and mutual good feeling, so that any real disagreement looks like a failure of it

names.name: Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, bishop of Carthage (248/249-258)

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop, chosen while still new to the faith, over his own reluctance. During a plague he taught us to love even our enemies. He was put to death under Valerian.

dates.display: a trained rhetorician who turned from a public career to Christian life, converted c. 246; ordained and elected bishop of Carthage between roughly July 248 and April 249 by the acclamation of the Carthaginian people, over the recorded opposition of five presbyters, while still newly baptised, as his deacon Pontius tells it; banished to Curubis under the Valerianic persecution; executed under the emperor Valerian in 258

names.name: Augustinius of Hippo Regius, presbyter 391, bishop 395/396-430

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop at Hippo. The people seized him and brought him to be made a presbyter while he wept. Later they pressed him into the bishop's office over his own refusal. He spent his last days weeping over psalms of penitence, while an army lay outside the walls.

dates.display: converted 386, baptised 387; seized by the congregation at Hippo and ordained presbyter against his own wishes in 391, weeping through it (Possidius, Vita IV); designated coadjutor and consecrated bishop of Hippo by Megalius, primate of Numidia, in 395/396, again amid popular acclamation (Possidius, Vita VIII); died 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo
